To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

black women with breast cancers have lower incidence of ER positivity, higher incidence of poorly and undifferentiated tumors and a higher incidence of patients discovered at more advanced stages of the disease than the national norm.

the ER and PgR status of breast cancer patients in the black population of the United States differs from the national norms in the following respects: a low incidence of positive ER tumors (46%), a high incidence of negative ER tumors (42%), a high incidence (55%) of poorly differentiated tumors and a low incidence (5.5 %) of well differentiated tumors, and a high incidence of advanced stage tumors at diagnosis (stage 3 and 4).
the incidence of poorly differentiated breast cancer and estrogen receptor negativity in black women with breast carcinoma was higher than in white women.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of breast cancer in black patients.
identifying the biological and clinical characteristics of breast cancer in black women, which may help to improve the management of breast cancer in this population.
the identification of factors that may contribute to the relatively poorer survival rate in black breast cancer patients compared to whites.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the incidence of breast cancer in the black population is increasing and the survival is decreasing.
the distribution of ER, PgR and tumor grade in black patients with breast cancer is not significantly different from that reported from other institutions on patients of other ethnic groups.
the incidence of ER positivity in black women with breast tumors is lower than that in white women, and this is associated with a higher incidence of tumors of poor differentiation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the distribution of ER‐positive tumors in black patients is similar to reports from white patients, however, a high percentage of ER‐negative tumors is observed.

the distribution of ER, PgR and tumor grade in black women with breast carcinoma is different from that in white women, and this difference may be one of the factors contributing to the relatively poorer survival rates in black women with this disease.

the distribution of ER, PgR and tumor differentiation in black breast cancer is not significantly different from that reported in white patients, with the exception of the higher percentage of ER‐negative tumors and poorly differentiated tumors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution of ER in black women with breast carcinoma does not differ from the national norm, but that the distribution of PgR differs.
black women with breast cancers are more likely to be diagnosed with a more advanced stage and a more aggressive tumor than their Caucasian counterparts.
black women have a lower incidence of ER‐pos breast cancer compared to their white counterparts.
